column3: For ephemeris-meridian elements, the observer's west longitude shifted by $(1.002738\times15/3600)\Delta T$ degrees, with ΔT in seconds. This accounts for Earth rotation when combining longitude with the tabulated hour angle μ and must not be applied again to elements already computed with UT1.

The penumbral and umbral cone radii at the observer's own plane, $L' = L - \zeta\tan f$, where $\zeta$ is the observer's height above the fundamental plane along the axis. $L_2'$ is negative inside the umbra (total) and positive inside the antumbra (annular).

$u = x - \xi$ and $v = y - \eta$ are the shadow axis position relative to the observer in the observer's plane, $m = \sqrt{u^2 + v^2}$ is their distance and $n$ the relative speed in Earth radii per hour. Contacts occur when $m$ equals $L_1'$ or $|L_2'|$.
The angle with $\sin\psi = \Delta/L$, where $\Delta$ is the perpendicular distance from the observer to the relative path of the shadow axis. The semi-duration of a phase is $L\cos\psi/n$.

The angle of a contact point on the solar limb, measured eastward from celestial north. The local formulas use P. The 1961 Explanatory Supplement calls it Q, distinct from this site's Q for global shadow-edge geometry.

The contact position angle measured counter-clockwise from the zenith point of the solar disc, $V=P-q_{\mathrm{par}}$ with $q_{\mathrm{par}}$ the parallactic angle. Some calculators report it as a clock-face hour.

The angle at the Sun between celestial north and the zenith. Here $q_{\mathrm{par}}=\operatorname{atan2}(\xi,\eta)$ in fundamental-plane coordinates. The Supplement's source-local symbol C differs from this site's C for the offset in Herald's limb construction.

The fraction of the solar diameter covered by the Moon at maximum eclipse. In the partial phase it is $(L_1' - m)/(L_1' + L_2')$. Inside the umbra or antumbra NASA reports instead the ratio of the apparent lunar to solar diameters, $(L_1' - L_2')/(L_1' + L_2')$.

Points of photospheric light shining through valleys on the lunar limb in the seconds around second and third contact. Their times at a site follow from the limb profile evaluated at each position angle.

Referred to the observer's actual position on the Earth's surface rather than to the Earth's centre. Topocentric positions include diurnal parallax and, for the Moon, differ from geocentric ones by up to about one degree.

Half the angular diameter of a body as seen by the observer, arcsin(R / distance), where R is the adopted physical radius. Contacts occur when the separation of the centres equals the sum or difference of the two semidiameters.

Position angle on the lunar disc measured from the Moon's north pole of rotation eastward, the coordinate against which limb-profile heights are tabulated. It differs from the celestial position angle by the position angle of the lunar axis.
